Learning Objectives
Understand modes of bone healing and the cellular mechanisms underlying the process.
Understand the uses of various bone grafts and bone graft substitutes, including the
advantages and disadvantages of each.
Understand the role of chemical factors in stimulating bone growth and healing.
Understand the use of external bone stimulators for enhancement of fracture healing.

Woven bone
Lamellar bone
Bone Cells
Bone contains three distinct cell types.
Osteoblasts
Cuboidal cells located along the bone surface comprising 4% to 6% of the total resident
bone cells
Form bone through the synthesis of bone matrix
Derived from bone marrow stromal cells through the expression of specific genes,
including bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) and members of the Wingless pathway1
Endosteal/periosteal bone lining cells
Quiescent flat-shaped cells of osteoblastic origin that cover bone surfaces in which neither
bone resorption or bone formation occurs
Bone lining cells are thought to play an important role in bone remodeling. It is
hypothesized that these cells prevent the interaction between osteoclasts and bone matrix
to prevent bone resorption when it should not occur but also promote the differentiation
of hematopoietic progenitor cells into osteoclasts. In addition, after osteoclastic bone
resorption, they prepare the surface of the bone for subsequent deposition of a thin layer
of collagen.1
Osteoclasts
Multinucleated macrophage-like cells that originate from mononuclear cells of the
hematopoietic progenitor cells lineage. Osteoclast differentiation and activation are
affected by cytokine and growth factors, notably receptor activator of nuclear factor-kappa
? ligand and macrophage colony-stimulating factor.2 The primary role of osteoclasts in
bone repair and remodeling is the resorption of bone matrix through the production of
proteolytic enzymes.
Osteocytes
Mature osteoblasts located within lacunae surrounded by mineralized bone matrix. They
make up more than 95% of total bone cells.
Osteocytes act as mechanoreceptors and help bone adapt to daily mechanical forces via
the regulation of osteoblast and osteoclast activity in bone remodeling.1

Bone Healing
Primary bone healing
Occurs if anatomic reduction and absolute stability are achieved with rigid fixation to
produce an environment of low interfragmentary strain. Direct contact must be present
between fractured bone ends such that osteoclasts and osteoblasts can restore lamellar
bone structure.
Primary bone healing can occur via contact healing or gap healing.
Contact healing requires the gap between bone ends to be less than 0.01 mm and
interfragmentary strain to be less than 2%. Cutting cones, remodeling units formed at the
end of the osteons near the fracture, consist of osteoclasts that resorb cortical bone to
create longitudinal cavities that cross the fracture site and allow for the deposition of
angiogenic factors and progenitor cells at the site of injury. Osteoprogenitor cells
differentiate into osteoblasts that lay down bone to bridge the fracture gap. Simultaneous
bony union and restoration of the haversian system occurs without the formation of
periosteal callus.
Gap healing requires two processes to restore the normal anatomic and biomechanical
properties of bone. Lamellar bone is initially laid down perpendicular to the anatomic axis of
the bone followed by a secondary remodeling process in which the primary, mechanically
weaker, bone structure is replaced by longitudinally oriented lamellar bone. Gap healing
differs from contact healing in that bony remodeling and haversian remodeling do not occur
simultaneously. The gap between fracture ends must be less than 1 mm.
Secondary bone healing
Secondary bone healing occurs through a cartilage intermediate via endochondral and
intramembranous ossification; both types of healing may occur concurrently at a fracture
site. Secondary bone healing requires relative stability and interfragmentary motion at the
fracture site to facilitate the production of soft callus. Secondary healing occurs in the
presence of an intermediate amount of strain (5% to 10%).
Secondary fracture healing can be described in four overlapping phases.
Hematoma formation
Bleeding from fracture ends and surrounding soft tissue forms a hematoma that fills the
fracture gap and acts as a temporary scaffolding for stem cell differentiation into fibrous
tissue, cartilage, and bone.
Rich in growth factors that are important for the migration and differentiation of
mesenchymal stem/progenitor cells (MSCs), angiogenesis, and initiating the inflammatory

9/3/26, 3:59 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001006
3/32

phase
Removal of hematoma may impair bone healing.
Inflammatory phase
Neutrophils, macrophages, and other inflammatory cells, including B-cells and T-cells,
infiltrate the hematoma and release inflammatory cytokines and growth factors, including
tumor necrosis factor-alpha; interleukin-1, -6, -11, and -18; transforming growth factor-
beta (TGF-ß), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), and fibroblast growth factor.
Together, these promote the production of a primary cartilaginous callus and
angiogenesis.
Recruitment of MSCs is thought to be mediated by stromal cell-derived factor 1 and
BMPs.
Reparative phase
Fibrocartilaginous callus formation (soft callus)
Fibrin-rich granulation tissue forms within the fracture hematoma.
MSCs recruited to the area differentiate to fibroblasts, chondroblasts, and osteoblasts.
Chondrogenesis produces a collagen-rich fibrocartilaginous network spanning the
fracture ends with a surrounding hyaline cartilage sleeve.
Fibrocartilage provides a framework for endochondral ossification that bridges the
fracture fragments.
Hard callus
Via intramembranous ossification, hard callus is formed adjacent to the fracture ends,
and the cartilaginous callus is gradually resorbed and replaced with woven bone.
Wingless pathway signaling regulates the differentiation of osteoprogenitor cells into
osteoblasts.
Macrophage colony-stimulating factor, receptor activator of nuclear factor-kappa B
ligand, osteoprotegrin, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha initiate resorption of
mineralized cartilage
Remodeling phase
A process that couples the resorption of woven bone with the deposition of lamellar bone
via osteoclast and osteoblast activation
Remodeling is mediated via biochemical signals, including interleukin-1 and tumor
necrosis factor-alpha, and via electrical polarity created by mechanical loading.
Impaired bone healing
Impaired bone healing is an ongoing problem in orthopaedic surgery. Among the 6.2 million
fractures occurring annually in the United States, 5% to 10% result in delayed union or

nonunion. This is associated with a substantial cost in terms of expense to the national
healthcare system and work force loss.3
The diamond concept is a popular conceptual framework for understanding the minimal
requirements for bone healing. It gives equal weight to the biologic environment (presence
of osteoinductive mediators, osteogenic cells, osteoconductive matrix) and mechanical
stability while recognizing the importance of systemic factors and local blood supply.4
Risk factors often are classified as patient-dependent and patient-independent factors (Table

Bone Graft and Bone Graft Substitutes
Bone graft procedures are increasingly used in traumatology, tumor surgery, spinal surgery,
infection, and revision arthroplasty to aid in the management of bone defects, bone healing,
and fusion. Bone has the capacity to heal and remodel; however, in patients with a critical-
sized defect or inadequate biology, successful healing may require the use of bone graft or
other bone healing adjuncts.
Bone is the second most transplanted tissue after blood. More than 500,000 bone graft
procedures are performed in the United States each year, with an associated cost estimated to
be higher than $3 billion.5,6
Bone grafts are implanted materials that promote bone healing and provide structural support
via their osteogenic, osteoinductive, and osteoconductive properties.

Osteogenic graft
Material that provides cells capable of de novo bone formation, in particular MSCs,
osteoblasts, and osteocytes.
Osteoconductive graft
Material that provides a scaffold that can facilitate bone formation. The three-dimensional
configuration and building-block material dictates osteoconductive properties.
Osteoinductive graft
Material containing growth factors that recruit MSCs and stimulate them to proliferate and
differentiate into chondroblasts and osteoblasts
Bone Graft Materials
Three major categories of bone graft exist: autogenous bone graft, allograft, and bone graft
substitutes. These arise from various sources and exhibit heterogeneous properties. They can
be used in isolation or can be combined into a composite graft (Table 2).
The current preferred bone graft is autologous bone graft because it is nonimmunogenic and
has osteogenic, osteoinductive, and osteoconductive properties; however, procurement of
autologous bone graft involves a surgical procedure associated with donor-site morbidity and
expense and may be limited by available graft volume. In response to these limitations,
allograft and bone graft substitutes also may be used.

Autograft
Tissue transferred from one site to another in the same individual
Autograft material usually is well incorporated and undergoes less resorption than allograft
because of histocompatibility of the tissue, the presence of viable cells, and greater
osteoinductivity and osteoconductivity.
May be in the form of cortical, cancellous, or corticocancellous graft
Cortical autograft
Nonvascularized graft
Primarily osteoconductive, provides excellent mechanical support
Poor cellularity limits its osteogenic and osteoinductive potential
Incorporation of the graft occurs via a process known as creeping substitution, which is a
slow, near-complete resorption of the graft that is predominately mediated by osteoclasts
with simultaneous deposition of new bone.
Vascularized cortical autograft
Commonly harvested from the fibula, iliac crest, distal radius, or rib
Nutrient, metaphysical, and/or perforating vessels are preserved and anastomosed to
vessels at the recipient site.
Osteogenic and osteoinductive cells are preserved, allowing graft incorporation to occur via
primary and secondary bone healing.
Vascularized versus nonvascularized grafts
During the initial 6 weeks after transplantation, vascularized grafts are mechanically
stronger because they undergo direct bony healing without bony resorption as a result of
maintained blood supply.7
Nonvascularized grafts undergo a period of necrosis and revascularization during the first 6
weeks after transplantation; however, animal model studies have suggested that their
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:59 PM

mechanical strength is similar to vascularized grafts after 6 months, and they are
histologically the same at 1 year.8
Indications
Nonvascularized grafts: defects 6 to 12 cm requiring structural support
Vascularized cortical autograft: defects larger than12 cm; high failure rate of
nonvascularized grafts in defects of this size
Cancellous autograft
Commonly harvested from the iliac crest, femur, proximal tibia, distal radius, or olecranon
Provides less structural support but contains a large number of osteoblasts, MSCs, BMPs,
and growth factors and typically provides an excellent scaffold for vascular ingrowth and
infiltration7
Iliac crest bone graft (ICBG)
The iliac crest is the most common donor site for autogenous bone graft because of easy
access and availability of fair quantities of cortical and cancellous bone.
It can be harvested from the anterior and posterior iliac crest via open or minimally
invasive procedures. In general, if considerable cancellous bone or corticocancellous bone
graft is required, an open technique is required. If more cancellous bone is required, it is
harvested from the posterior iliac crest because this region provides up to three time more
cancellous bone than the anterior iliac crest.9
Major limitations to ICBG are available volume and donor-site morbidity. Reported
complications include infection, hematoma, seroma, postoperative pain, scar sensitivity,
and injury to the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve. The most common complications are
donor-site pain and sensory disturbances.10
Substantial heterogeneity in the reported morbidity rates exists because of differences in
patient populations, procedures, and surgical technique.
Minor complications are reported in 10% to 39% of patients, whereas major
complications, such as pseudoaneurysm, pelvic instability, avulsion of the anterior
superior iliac spine, hernia, and arteriovenous fistula, are reported in 0.75% to 25% of
patients.9
In a systematic review of the literature, the overall complication rate was 19%, with the
incidence of chronic donor-site pain and sensory disturbances being 7.75% and 4.81%,
respectively.9 Although the overall complication rate between anterior and posterior iliac
crest donor sites was not substantially different, the rates of infection, hematoma
formation, fracture, and hypertrophic scar were more common if the graft was harvested

from the anterior iliac crest; however, chronic donor-site pain and sensory disturbances
were lower. The discrepancy between anterior and posterior donor-site pain may be
because most patients who had graft harvested from the posterior iliac crest were
undergoing reconstructive spine surgery, which tends to be associated with higher rates
of donor-site pain. This may be a result of the performed procedure and patients’ inability
to differentiate pain originating from the graft site from postoperative pain.11
In a prospective study assessing donor-site morbidity among orthopaedic trauma
patients after anterior ICBG, no major complications were noted, and persistent pain at
the iliac crest donor site occurred in only 2% of patients 1 year postoperatively,
suggesting the procedure is well tolerated among certain patient populations.12
Surgical technique has been shown to reduce donor-site morbidity. Various surgical
techniques, the manner in which the cortices are managed after harvest, and post-
harvest reconstruction of the ilium may reduce donor-site complications, particularly the
incidence and severity of pain.9
Reamer-irrigator-aspirator (RIA) graft
Recently, RIA has become a popular method for harvesting cancellous autograft from the
medullary canal of long bones because the liquid filtrate and the particulate aspirate
possess osteogenic and osteoinductive properties. Although this device was initially
developed to minimize the physiologic sequelae of pressurization during reaming of long-
bone fractures (increased intramedullary pressure, heat production, surgical time, and fat
embolism), it has been found to be a valuable tool for harvesting autologous bone graft.
Obtaining bone graft with the use of an RIA is an attractive alternative to iliac crest because
it is associated with decreased donor-site morbidity, pain, and wound complications and
may provide increased graft volume13,14 (Table 3).

Biologic activity of RIA graft
The biologic activity and cellular composition of RIA graft appears to be comparable to
that of ICBG. Samples of RIA graft have been shown to have greater expression of genes
associated with vascular, skeletal, and hematopoietic tissue than material from the iliac
crest. In particular, the greater expression of BMPs and vascular endothelial growth factor
receptors present in RIA graft may make the cells more responsive to osteogenic and
angiogenic growth stimulation compared with cells in ICBG.15 In addition, stem cell
markers and growth factors necessary for bone formation, including fibroblast growth
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:59 PM
AAOS | Bone Healing and Bone Grafts
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001006
13/32

factor-alpha, PDGF, insulin-like growth factor-1, TGF-ß1, and BMP-2 are more abundant in
RIA graft.10
Obtaining bone graft with the use of an RIA appears to induce higher cell stress levels in
freshly collected progenitor cells compared with progenitor cells harvested from the iliac
crest; however, this appears to be temporary and reversible because the proliferative
potential and osteogenesis of MSCs from RIA waste and iliac crest bone marrow are
comparable.16
Bone healing and adverse events
The rate of bony union and complication rate associated with RIA graft is comparable with
that of ICBG; however, RIA graft is associated with lower postoperative donor-site
morbidity.14
RIA appears to be a safe method of obtaining autologous bone graft. The reported
complication rate associated with RIA is lower than that associated with ICBG.
Complications include cortical penetration during reaming, donor-site fracture, donor-
site infection, heterotopic ossification, and considerable intraoperative blood loss. In the
largest case series to date, Qvick et al17 retrospectively reviewed 204 RIA procedures in
184 patients and reported a complication rate of 1.96%. These complications were
secondary to donor-site fracture and intraoperative cortical perforation. Similar rates
have been reported in smaller case series.
Although the rate of major complications is low, RIA is associated with considerable
intraoperative blood loss. The mean estimated blood loss among patients undergoing
RIA has been reported to be 674 mL (range, 100 to 2,000 mL) compared with a mean
intraoperative blood loss of 255 mL (50 to 1,000 mL) for ICBG (P < 0.001). As many as
44% of patients undergoing RIA require a blood transfusion and experience a mean
hematocrit level drop of 13.7%.18
Autologous bone marrow aspirate (BMA)
BMA is a potential source of MSCs and osteoprogenitors. It may be aspirated
percutaneously from the iliac crest, vertebral body, or other sources. BMA can be used
alone or mixed with other bone graft extenders and ceramics to create a composite graft
material.
Although initially thought to have a high concentration of osteoprogenitor cells, some
recent studies have suggested the opposite. Therefore, the role of BMA in bone healing
may be related to the relatively high concentration of endothelial progenitor cells and their
ability to stimulate angiogenesis.19

The efficacy of BMA appears to be directly related to the number of progenitor cells present
in the graft and the need for the aspirate to be concentrated to achieve the baseline
number of cells necessary for osteogenesis (>1,500 progenitors/cm3).20 The number of
cells harvested varies between patients and is affected by age, sex, local and systemic
disease, and appropriate aspiration technique.
The use of BMA concentrate alone or in combination with an osteoconductive and/or
osteoinductive substrate to form a composite graft has shown promising results in the
management of long-bone nonunions. In a recent retrospective cohort study, no
considerable difference in union rate was reported between long-bone nonunions
managed via ICBG or BMA concentrate with allograft.21
Allograft
Tissue from genetically nonidentical subjects from the same species
Allograft can be categorized as corticocancellous and cortical grafts, osteochondral and
whole-body segments, morcellized and cancellous chips, or demineralized bone matrix
(DBM).22
Compared with autogenous bone graft, which contains osteogenic and osteoinductive cells,
allograft is primarily osteoconductive because living osteogenic cells are removed during
the process of sterilization, which is required to reduce the risk of disease transmission and
an immune response.
The extent of osteoconductive properties and mechanical strength depends, in part, on the
method of graft processing and whether the graft is cortical or cancellous bone.
Lack of donor-site morbidity, large graft volume, generally successful outcomes, and
decreased surgical times make allograft a popular alternative to autologous bone graft;
however, lack of osteogenic capability; high costs; and risks, such as viral transmission,
make allograft an imperfect substitute.
A risk of disease transmission or infection always exists with the use of donor material.
Strict screening, proper procurement, and processing for donated tissue regulation and
techniques are continually advancing and enforced by qualified agencies.
Several types of allograft may be considered.
Fresh allograft
Rarely used because of the potential for an immune response and disease transmission,
host versus graft disease• Fresh allograft may be processed to remove cells and reduce
host immune reaction. This process has been shown to improve incorporation.
Fresh-frozen washed allograft

9/3/26, 3:59 PM
AAOS | Bone Healing and Bone Grafts
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001006
15/32

Reduces immunogenicity; frozen allograft requires cold storage logistics and rewarming
(ie, saline) before implantation to avoid brittleness, which may result in longitudinal
fractures.
For sterilization, obtained materials are cleaned with the use of chemicals or irradiation.
Chemical washing is preferred because of mechanical weakness after irradiation.
Osteoconductive properties and some limited osteoinductive capabilities are
maintained.
The shelf life of fresh-frozen bone maintained at -20°C and -70°C is 1 year and 5 years,
respectively.
Freeze-dried washed allograft
Has properties similar to those of frozen allograft, with a few exceptions
Prepared by freeze-drying (lyophilization): freezing the bone, placing it under a vacuum,
and obtaining direct conversion of ice to vapor
For sterilization, obtained materials are cleaned using chemical solutions, such as
aqueous solutions of detergents, surfactants, hydrogen peroxides, organic solvents,
acids, alcohol, etc.
Stored at room temperature
The shelf life of freeze-dried bone is indefinite; however, the sterilization of the
packaging may expire.
Because of the preparation process of drying, biomechanical studies have
demonstrated a similar compressive and tensile strength as frozen bone but reduced
torsional/bending strength compared to fresh or fresh-frozen bone. This is not suitable
for structural grafting.
DBM
DBM is an allograft derivative produced via acid extraction of allograft bone. It contains
proteins, collagen, and growth factors (BMP, TGF-ß, insulin-like growth factors).
It is osteoconductive and serves as a scaffold for new bone formation; however,
because of the demineralization process, it lacks structural support.
Theoretically, it has osteoinductive properties because of retained growth factors;
however, its osteoinductive capacity varies because of differences in processing and
individual donor characteristics.
DBM frequently is used as a bone graft extender and is mixed with autograft, BMA,
and/or isolated native blood-derived growth factors to stimulate new bone growth.
Limited clinical evidence supports the use of DBM; however, more recently, DBM has
been combined with viable bone matrices to form cellular bone allograft. These contain

with autograft harvest. The use of cellular bone allograft in foot and ankle arthrodesis
and single-level anterior cervical diskectomy and fusion for patients with a degenerative
spine has shown promising results, with fusion rates comparable to, or higher than,
arthrodesis rates with the use of autograft.23-25
Bone Graft Substitutes
Bone graft substitutes can be defined as a synthetic, inorganic, or biologically organic
combination that can be inserted for the management of a bone defect rather than
autogenous or allogenous bone.26
Major advantages of bone graft substitutes are ease of use, avoidance of possible donor-site
morbidity, avoidance of disease transmission associated with autograft and allograft use,
and reduced surgical time.
The ideal bone graft material should be biocompatible, osteoconductive, osteoinductive,
osteogenic, and resorbable/degradable with mechanical properties similar to those of bone,
such that it is able to provide temporary, mechanical support; however, bone graft substitutes
primarily are osteoconductive because they lack osteoinductive and osteogenic cells. The
porosity and pore size of synthetic grafts are designed to be similar to that of native bone to
allow for cellular attachment and proliferation; however, although the porous nature of these
materials facilitates new tissue ingrowth and vascularization, it compromises the mechanical
strength and structural integrity of the graft.
Inorganic bone graft substitutes
Bioceramics
Bioceramics alone possess no osteogenic or osteoinductive properties, and they have
variable immediate structural support secondary to their rate of resorption.
Calcium sulfate
Resistant to compressive force, but poor tensile strength
Weaker than cortical bone but stronger compressive strength than cancellous bone;
therefore, they may provide some stability while new bone forms. Calcium sulfate is
reabsorbed in 1 to 3 months; therefore, caution should be exercised in populations in
which bone healing is expected to be delayed because it may result in fixation failure (eg,
elderly patients, large bone defects).

Calcium phosphate
Calcium phosphate may increase immediate load-bearing capabilities by enhancing the
structural integrity of fracture fixation. Biomechanical studies comparing the fatigue
strength of calcium phosphate–augmented fixation with autogenous bone graft–
augmented fixation in lateral tibial plateau fractures reported substantially higher fatigue
strength and ultimate load in calcium phosphate repairs compared with autogenous bone
graft repair.27
Hydroxyapatite
Major mineral component of bone
Synthetic hydroxyapatite has the chemical formula Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2. It typically is used in
its crystalline form and is nondegradable.
Marine coral is converted from its calcium carbonate skeleton to hydroxyapatite via a
hydrothermal conversion technique or high-temperature sintering.
The porosity of marine coral is similar to that of cancellous bone, with a pore size of 500
μm. The resultant porosity of hydroxyapatite allows for cellular ingrowth.
Hydroxyapatite has good compressive strength but low tensile strength.
Hydroxyapatite is poorly reabsorbed. Therefore, it does not facilitate new bone growth or
remodeling and may increase the risk of fracture around the hydroxyapatite bone
substitute.
Tricalcium phosphate
Commercially available as beta tricalcium phosphate (ß-Ca3[PO4]2; ß-TCP)
Slower resorption than calcium sulfate, which allows a balance between new bone
formation and graft absorption
Compressive strength greater than that of cancellous bone
Biphasic bioceramics
Mixture of ß-TCP and hydroxyapatite or calcium sulfate and hydroxyapatite
In a recent prospective, multicenter randomized controlled trial, the use of biphasic
hydroxyapatite and calcium sulfate was noninferior to autologous bone graft with regard to
patient-reported outcomes, the rate of fracture healing, remodeling, and articular
subsidence.28

Bioactive glass is synthetic, silica (SiO2)-based substances that are designed to interact with
the surrounding biologic environment to form chemical bonds between the material
surface and the surrounding bone and soft tissue. Formation of a carbonated
hydroxyapatite layer provides the bonding interface with bone and soft tissue. The ion
dissolution products of bioactive glass (eg, silica, calcium, phosphorus, and sodium) affect
the gene expression of osteoblasts, contributing to its regenerative ability.29
Bioactive glass has been used for various clinical applications since first discovered by
Hench in 1969. Many types of bioactive glasses (45S5, S53P4) are available, and glass-based
products can be used in head and neck surgery, periodontal procedures, and orthopaedic
procedures.
Because of its relatively poor mechanical properties (brittleness, low bending strength, and
fracture toughness), the applications of bioactive glass are limited to non–load-bearing
implants.
Based on animal studies, the rate of bone formation is related to the bioactivity of the
material, specifically the rate of surface reactions and the rate of dissolution of silica.30 The
most critical feature for bioactivity is silica content lower than 60% in weight.31
Orthobiologic Factors
Bone Morphogenetic Proteins
BMPs were first identified in 1965 by Marshall Urist. He discovered a substance in DBM that
had the ability to induce osteogenesis if implanted in extra-skeletal tissue.
BMPs are members of the TGF-ß superfamily and play an important role in embryologic
development and a major role in skeletal remodeling and repair. BMPs are considered to be
the most potent osteoinductive agents and are responsible for the migration, proliferation,
and differentiation of progenitor cells. More than 20 proteins have been identified, most
notably BMP-2 and BMP-7.
Early evidence suggested that synthetic BMPs could promote the growth of large volumes of
bone and were effective adjuncts in bone healing of nonunion, bone defects, and spinal
fusion; however, subsequent studies have failed to confirm their superiority or noninferiority
to autologous bone graft.
Their use in clinical practice remains controversial because of a paucity of clear evidence in
level I clinical trials supporting their use; high associated costs; and documented side effects
and safety concerns, including carcinogenesis.

As previously discussed by Nauth et al,32 several issues related to the use of recombinant
human BMPs (rhBMPs) have reduced the initial enthusiasm for their use in bone
regeneration. First, the degree to which they can build bone by themselves remains unclear.
rhBMPs possess primarily osteoinductive properties; therefore, their success depends on the
presence of osteoprogenitor cells and adequate blood supply at the desired site of bone
regeneration. In addition, rhBMP can activate osteoclast pathways, resulting in possible bone
resorption and osteolysis. Second, rhBMP is relatively soluble and requires a carrier to
contain the material at the intended site of use and prevent diffusion into adjacent tissues;
however, even in the presence of a delivery system, supraphysiologic doses are required to
achieve the desired osteogenic effects, increasing cost and the risk of side effects. Third, an
understanding regarding the ideal dosing, timing of administration, and indications for
combinations with other graft materials currently is lacking. Lastly, the carcinogenic potential
of rhBMPs continues to be a subject of debate in the literature.
rhBMP-2
rhBMP-2 is the only approved rhBMP currently on the market. The concentration of rhBMP-2
is 1.5 mg/mL after reconstitution, and rhBMP-2 is delivered on an absorbable collagen
sponge. In 2002, rhBMP-2 was approved by the FDA for limited applications in single-level
anterior lumbar interbody fusion. In 2004, the FDA expanded the approved indications to
include the management of acute open tibia fractures.In 2007, rhBMP-2 was approved as an
alternative to autogenous bone grafting for sinus and localized alveolar ridge
augmentation.33
rhBMP-2 and fractures
In 2002, a randomized controlled study comparing the management of tibial shaft
fractures via rhBMP-2 and intramedullary nailing with the standard of care
(intramedullary nailing) reported that rhBMP-2 was safe and effective in accelerating
healing of tibial shaft fractures.34 In 2006, a subgroup analysis of these data reported that
the addition of rhBMP-2 considerably reduced the frequency of bone grafting procedures
and other secondary treatment options for the management of type III tibial fractures.35
However, in 2011, a repeat randomized controlled trial reported that the addition of
rhBMP-2 to reamed intramedullary nailing during tibial shaft fracture fixation did not
accelerate healing but was associated with higher rates of infection. In fact, the trial was
terminated early because of an imbalance in infection rates between the treatment
groups.36 Similarly, enrollment was suspended in a follow-up study assessing the efficacy
of rhBMP-2 in tibial shaft fractures because of the lack of efficacy.37

rhBMP-2 and spinal fusion
Results from early clinical trials assessing the effect of rhBMP-2 on anterior lumbar
interbody fusion reported higher rates of fusion with rhBMP-2 compared with ICBG, with
no difference reported in adverse outcomes.38-40 These studies resulted in FDA approval
of rhBMP-2 for use in spine fusions that involved anterior lumbar interbody fusion.
A recent meta-analysis assessing the effect of ICBG versus rhBMP-2 on fusion rates in
patients who underwent posterolateral fusion of the lumbar spine reported that rhBMP-2
may have a role in spinal fusion. The use of rhBMP-2 was associated with higher fusion
rates, decreased surgical time, decreased intraoperative blood loss, and decreased length
of hospital stay, with higher revision surgery rates in the ICBG group; however, patient-
reported outcomes assessing quality of life were the same between the groups. The rate
of adverse events between the two groups were not substantially different, suggesting
BMP-2 use is relatively safe; however, , the rate of cancer was 2.5 times higher in the BMP
group than in the ICBG group (statistically significant).41
Adverse effects and safety
Initial clinical trials on the use of rhBMP-2 suggested that the adverse-effect profile was
minimal; however, several well-documented adverse effects have emerged, including
postoperative inflammation and associated adverse effects (eg, radiculitis, anterior
cervical spine swelling causing dysphagia), ectopic bone formation, osteoclast-mediated
bone resorption, wound complications, and inappropriate adipogenesis (ie, bone cyst
formation).42 Postoperative edema is the most common complication, with the
incidence in lumbar and nonlumbar procedures being approximately 30% and
approximately 64%, respectively.43
A likely contributor to the wide adverse-effect profile is the fact that BMPs frequently are
used for off-label applications. Initial FDA clearance was for limited applications in
nonunion and spinal fusion; however, 85% of BMP use is reported to be off-label.44 In
addition, the use of supraphysiologic doses to achieve the desired osteogenic effect
likely contributes to the high rates of adverse effects. Unfortunately, the optimal dose in
humans is unknown and currently is based on primate efficacy testing.
The association between the use of rhBMP-2 and carcinogenesis is controversial. The
oncologic concerns of rhBMP-2 use are related to basic science research that has
demonstrated a relationship between BMP signaling and breast, lung, pancreatic,
prostate, and oral squamous cell carcinoma. BMPs regulate many cellular processes,

rhBMP-7 (osteogenic protein-1) initially received limited FDA approval under a Humanitarian
Device Exemption for the management of recalcitrant tibial nonunions; however, it failed to
gain FDA premarket approval in 2009, and its sale was discontinued in 2014.33
rhBMP-7 primarily has been studied in the context of nonunion. In the first clinical trial
assessing rhBMP-7, no substantial difference in union rates was reported between
autologous bone graft and osteogenic protein-1 in the management of tibial nonunions.45

patients with degenerative spondylolisthesis failed to show the superiority of osteogenic
protein-1 over autologous bone graft.46
rhBMP-6
The osteoinductive potential of rhBMP-2 and rhBMP-7 in the healing of spinal fusions and
long-bone fractures has not been borne out in the literature for hand, wrist, or forearm
fractures and nonunions.47,48
Recently, the use of a novel autologous bone graft substitute consisting of rhBMP-6
dispersed within an autologous blood coagulum has been described.49 In animal models,
rhBMP-6 has been shown to be safe and effective in inducing new bone formation. The use
of autologous blood coagulum helps reduce the inflammatory and immune response
reported in commonly used animal-derived collagenous carriers (eg, bovine-sourced
absorbable collagen sponges), including anti-BMP antibodies, systemic BMP, and local
adverse effects (eg, ectopic bone formation, skin redness, and edema).50

Platelet-Derived Growth Factor
PDGF is a modulator of inflammation and tissue repair. It is made and stored in platelets and
released in the acute phase of the inflammatory response. PDGF promotes chemotaxis of
inflammatory cells, mitogenesis of MSCs, and angiogenesis; therefore, it is critical in the early
phases of the healing cascade and in the formation of soft callus.23
Commercially, recombinant human PDGF is packaged with ß-TCP to act as a scaffold for bone
formation because it lacks inherent osteoconductive properties.
The safety and efficacy of PDGF has been well documented in the foot and ankle literature,
with several randomized controlled trials documenting its ability to facilitate ankle and
hindfoot fusion at a level comparable with that of autologous bone graft.51 In a multicenter,
prospective randomized controlled trial, Daniels et al52 evaluated the efficacy and safety of
recombinant human PDGF in combination with an injectable, osteoconductive ß-TCP–collagen
matrix versus autograft in ankle and hindfoot fusions. The recombinant human PDGF /ß-TCP–
collagen treatment resulted in equivalent rates of joint fusion, radiologic outcomes, clinical
success, and functional patient improvement compared with the autograft treatment.
Other Modalities to Enhance Bone Healing
Electromagnetic stimulation
The use of electric stimulation in the management of fractures has been documented since
the mid 1800s. The first clinically important research on the influence of electricity on callus
formation in fracture healing was described in 1953 by Yasuda and later by Fakuda.
Bone tissue has bioelectric potential.
Bioelectric potential is electronegative in areas of growth or healing. The area returns to
neutral or electropositive as healing progresses.

Bioelectric potential is electronegative in areas of compression and electropositive in areas
of tension.
The application of an external electric charge is thought to enhance bone healing by inducing
a stronger net negative potential at the fracture site and stimulating the calcium-calmodulin
pathway secondary to the upregulation of BMPs, TGF-ß, and other cytokines.53
Types of stimulation
Pulsed electromagnetic field: noninvasive, external coil generates a broad electromagnetic
field that delivers widespread, pulsed electrical charges at the fracture site
Capacitive coupling: noninvasive, external capacitor delivers current between two external,
cutaneous electrodes placed on the skin near the fracture site to provide a concentrated
current at the fracture site
Direct current electrical stimulation: constant, uniform current is delivered at the fracture
site through implanted electrodes
Clinical efficacy (Table 4)
Considerable variability in outcomes among studies and lack of high-level evidence in the
literature makes determining the effectiveness of bone stimulation on fracture healing
inconclusive.
A paucity of high-quality level I evidence supports the use of electric stimulation in the
management of delayed union and nonunion of fractures. Although level I evidence
supports the use of capacitive coupling and pulsed electromagnetic field in the
management of nonunion, these studies have been criticized for their small sample sizes
and the presence of confounding variables.54
Level I evidence supports the use of capacitive coupling and pulsed electromagnetic field in
spinal fusion.54

Low-intensity pulsed ultrasonography (LIPUS)
The exact mechanism by which LIPUS affects fracture healing remains unclear.
1.5- to 3.0-MHz ultrasonic pulses are directly applied to the fracture site, creating
micromotion. This mechanical signal is converted to a biochemical signal inside the cell,
which is thought to stimulate signal transduction, blood flow, angiogenesis, and
osteogenic gene expression.55

In 1994, the FDA approved the use of LIPUS for accelerating healing of fresh fractures; in

Clinical efficacy
The reported efficacy of LIPUS depends on fracture location and type of fracture.
Level I evidence supports the use of LIPUS in certain fresh fractures, including distal
radius, scaphoid, and Jones fractures, as well as scaphoid non-union and distraction
osteogenesis; however, LIPUS does not appear to have a role in the management of
fresh clavicle fractures, tibial stress fractures, or fresh tibia fractures managed via
intramedullary nailing.54 In a large, multicenter randomized controlled trial assessing
the efficacy of LIPUS in patients with an open or closed tibia fracture who underwent
intramedullary nailing, LIPUS did not accelerate radiographic healing or improve
functional recovery.56
Several meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials have assessed the effect of LIPUS
on bone healing, reporting varying results. Although many meta-analyses determined
that LIPUS reduced time to fracture healing, the quality of the pooled data has
prevented any definitive conclusions. Recently, Schandelmaier et al57 reported that,
based on moderate to high quality evidence, LIPUS did not reduce time to return to
work or the number of subsequent surgical procedures. In addition, if only trials at low
risk of bias were considered, LIPUS did not reduce days to weight bearing, pain at 4 to 6
weeks postoperatively, or days to radiographic healing. Although Lou et al58 reported
